name: Feature Stores
title: Feature Stores
answer: A feature store is a managed set of tables of model input values, computed once and served identically to training and to production, which prevents a model from being trained on one definition of a value and run on another. It sits between raw data sources and the model, giving data scientists and engineers a shared catalog of features. The scope covers offline storage for training and online storage for low latency serving, plus the transformation logic that keeps both in sync. It also covers metadata, versioning, and lineage for each feature.

sections.body: A feature store is a managed set of tables of model input values, computed once and served identically to training and to production, which prevents a model from being trained on one definition of a value and run on another. It sits between raw data sources and the model, giving data scientists and engineers a shared catalog of features. The scope covers offline storage for training and online storage for low latency serving, plus the transformation logic that keeps both in sync. It also covers metadata, versioning, and lineage for each feature.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Feature stores typically run on a combination of a data warehouse or lakehouse for offline storage and a low latency database or key value store for online serving. Common backends include PostgreSQL, Redis, Cassandra, and cloud warehouse services. The site tracks 263 active Model Context Protocol servers for SQL databases and warehouses, which reflects how often feature stores are wired into SQL based data platforms. Every page on this site is itself built from a PostgreSQL database, a reminder that relational stores remain a practical foundation for metadata and offline tables.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with defining features as transformations over source tables, often in SQL or a dataframe API. A pipeline computes those transformations on a schedule or in streaming, writes the results to the offline store, and materializes the same values to the online store. Point in time correctness is enforced so that training rows only see feature values that were available at the time of the label. Teams then register features, document them, and reuse them across models. Monitoring checks for drift and skew between offline and online values.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers who can define, change, and read a feature, with access controls tied to the same identity systems used elsewhere. Provenance records which source tables, transformations, and code versions produced each feature value. Versioning lets a team roll back a feature definition without breaking models that depend on the old one. Audit trails show when a feature was updated and which training runs or production services consumed it. Because features can encode sensitive data, teams apply the same privacy and retention rules as the underlying tables.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Feature stores are moving toward tighter integration with the SQL and warehouse layer, so that definitions live close to the data and are governed by existing database permissions. Streaming and real time features are becoming more common as models need fresher inputs. The line between a feature store and a semantic layer or metrics layer is blurring, with shared catalogs and lineage. Expect more automation for backfills, skew detection, and cost control. Some teams are also exploring feature stores as a way to share reusable inputs across many models rather than rebuilding them per project.
